questions.text: Is your business in a federally regulated industry?
questions.help: Federally regulated workplaces follow the Canada Labour Code instead of provincial labour law. The government's list includes banks, air transportation, railways and road transport (trucks and buses) that cross provincial or international borders, marine shipping, ports and ferries, pipelines that cross borders, telecommunications, radio and television broadcasting, postal and courier services, grain elevators and feed mills, uranium mining and most federal Crown corporations. Most shops, restaurants, offices, builders and factories are provincially regulated: answer no.

questions.text: How many employees does the business have?
questions.help: Count everyone on the payroll, full-time, part-time and casual, each as one. Some rules count on their own day or place: Ontario's written-policy rules count employees in Ontario on January 1, British Columbia's pay transparency rule counts employees working in B.C. on January 1, and the federal rules use the average number of employees.

questions.text: Is it a private company (its shares are not listed on a stock exchange and it is not a reporting issuer)?
questions.help: Private companies must keep a register of the people who own or control them. Public companies and their wholly-owned subsidiaries are excused.

questions.text: Did it receive more than $10,000 in public donations or government grants in a single financial year?
questions.help: A federal not-for-profit corporation that does is called a soliciting corporation and must send its financial statements to Corporations Canada every year.

questions.text: Does the business hold personal information about customers, clients or other people?
questions.help: Names with contact details, payment details, health or identity information and similar records about people. If such information is lost, stolen or seen by someone who should not see it, privacy law can require a report.

questions.text: Do you send emails, texts or other electronic messages to promote your business?
questions.help: Newsletters, offers and other commercial messages sent to customers or prospects. Canada's anti-spam law sets rules for consent, for what each message must contain and for unsubscribe requests.

questions.text: Is the business in one of the sectors that must report to FINTRAC?
questions.help: FINTRAC's list: accountants and accounting firms (when carrying out certain activities for clients), real estate brokers, sales representatives and developers, dealers in precious metals and precious stones, money services businesses, mortgage administrators, brokers and lenders, securities dealers, life insurance companies, brokers and agents, casinos, cheque cashers, armoured car businesses, factors, financing or leasing entities, title insurers, British Columbia notaries, and banks, credit unions, trust and loan companies.

questions.text: Is it a money services business?
questions.help: Money services businesses must register with FINTRAC before they begin to operate and renew the registration every two years. If you are not sure whether your activities make you one, check FINTRAC's registration page.

questions.text: Does the business import or export commercial goods?
questions.help: Goods brought into or sent out of Canada for sale or business use. You need an import-export program account (RM) with the Canada Border Services Agency.

questions.text: Is the business owned or controlled by non-Canadians, and has it just started a new business activity in Canada or bought control of a Canadian business?
questions.help: A foreign investor files a notification under the Investment Canada Act each time it starts a new business activity in Canada or acquires control of an existing Canadian business (unless the investment is large enough to need a full review).

questions.text: Do you or your business own a trademark registered in Canada?
questions.help: A registered trademark has to be renewed, for a fee, every 10 years.

questions.text: Is it a large business that makes goods, or imports goods made outside Canada (or controls a business that does)?
questions.help: Large means it is listed on a Canadian stock exchange, or it has a place of business, does business or has assets in Canada and, in at least one of its last two financial years, met at least two of these three on its consolidated financial statements: $20 million or more in assets, $40 million or more in revenue, an average of 250 or more employees.

questions.text: Does the business administer an employee pension plan registered with the federal regulator (OSFI)?
questions.help: Pension plans registered under the federal Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 are supervised by OSFI. Plans registered with a province follow that province's rules instead.

questions.text: Does a facility of yours meet the reporting criteria of the National Pollutant Release Inventory?
questions.help: Broadly: employees and contractors at the facility work more than 20,000 hours in the year (about 10 full-time workers) and the facility makes, processes, uses or releases a listed substance above its threshold (for most substances, 10 tonnes at a concentration of 1% or more). Some activities, such as running stationary combustion equipment above the air-release thresholds, count whatever the hours. Environment and Climate Change Canada publishes the full test.

questions.text: Is the business holding money or other property that belongs to someone else and has gone unclaimed?
questions.help: Alberta calls a business that holds property for an owner a holder. Property left unclaimed for the period the law sets has to be reported and handed to the province.

compliances.name: Keep the register of individuals with significant control up to date and file changes
compliances.form: ISC register and ISC filing (Online Filing Centre)
compliances.head: Ownership register
compliances.brief: A private federal corporation keeps a register of its individuals with significant control (the people who own or control it) and files that information with Corporations Canada. Changes have to be recorded and filed quickly, not only once a year.
compliances.why: It is a private corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations created under the Canada Business Corporations Act, except reporting issuers, corporations listed on a designated stock exchange, Crown corporations and their wholly-owned subsidiaries.

due.text: Within 15 days of a change to the register

compliances.dueText: Update the register at least once a year and within 15 days of becoming informed of any change. File the change with Corporations Canada within 15 days of recording it in the register. The information is also filed every year with the annual return, and within 30 days of the date on a certificate of amalgamation.
compliances.penalty: A Certificate of Compliance may be refused, the corporation may be administratively dissolved, and it may be found guilty of an offence and fined up to $100,000 on summary conviction.
compliances.evidence: the corporation will need to file the change within 15 days of recording the change in their ISC register.
compliances.note: The yearly filing with the annual return is already covered by the existing item ca_corpcan. Who must keep the register was read on the page 'Individuals with significant control' (modified 2026-03-30).

compliances.name: Report a change of directors (federal corporation)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: When a director joins, leaves or changes address, a federal corporation tells Corporations Canada so the public record stays correct.
compliances.why: It is a corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act.

due.text: Within 15 days of a change in the board of directors

compliances.dueText: Within 15 days of new directors being elected or of individuals ceasing to be directors. A director's change of address: within 15 days of the corporation being informed of it.
compliances.evidence: You must notify Corporations Canada of any change in the board of directors within 15 days of the following actions:
compliances.note: The page states no fine for this filing; it describes dissolution only for unfiled annual returns and ISC information.

compliances.name: Report a change of registered office address (federal corporation)
compliances.form: Change of registered office address (Online Filing Centre)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A federal corporation that moves its registered office tells Corporations Canada.
compliances.why: It is a corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act.

due.text: Within 15 days following the change of address

compliances.dueText: You must notify Corporations Canada of any change to the corporation's registered office address within 15 days following the change.
compliances.evidence: You must notify Corporations Canada of any change to your corporation's registered office address ... within 15 days following the change.

compliances.name: Hold the annual shareholders' meeting (federal corporation)
compliances.head: Corporate governance
compliances.brief: A federal corporation holds a shareholders' meeting every year. At a minimum the meeting considers the financial statements.
compliances.why: It is a corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act.
compliances.dueText: On a date that is no later than 15 months after holding the last preceding annual meeting, but no later than six months after the end of its preceding financial year. The directors must call the first shareholders' meeting within 18 months of the date of incorporation.
compliances.evidence: must hold a shareholders' meeting on a date that is no later than 15 months after holding the last preceding annual meeting ... no later than six months after the end of its preceding financial year
compliances.note: The 18-month rule for the first meeting was read on 'Next steps following the incorporation of your business' (modified 2026-02-25). The page on shareholders was last modified 2023-05-10.

compliances.name: Report a change of directors or registered office (federal not-for-profit)
compliances.form: Changes regarding directors; change of registered office address (Online Filing Centre)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A federal not-for-profit corporation tells Corporations Canada when a director is appointed, elected, resigns, is removed or changes address, and when its registered office moves. Filing is free.
compliances.why: It is a not-for-profit corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act.

due.text: Within 15 days of a change regarding directors

compliances.dueText: Changes regarding directors: within 15 days of the change or, in the case of a change to a director's address, within 15 days of being notified of the change. Change of registered office address: immediately (it takes effect only once Corporations Canada accepts it).
compliances.penalty: Any not-for-profit corporation that defaults for a period of one year in sending any fee, notice or document required by the NFP Act could be dissolved.
compliances.evidence: Within 15 days of the change or, in the case of a change to a director's address, within 15 days of being notified of the change
compliances.note: The page was last modified 2022-07-21.

compliances.name: File new or changed by-laws (federal not-for-profit)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A federal not-for-profit corporation sends Corporations Canada a copy of every new by-law, every change and every repeal. Filing is free.
compliances.why: It is a not-for-profit corporation incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Corporations under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act that adopt, change or repeal a by-law.

due.text: Within 12 months of the members confirming the by-law

compliances.dueText: Within 12 months of confirmation by members.
compliances.penalty: Any not-for-profit corporation that defaults for a period of one year in sending any fee, notice or document required by the NFP Act could be dissolved.
compliances.evidence: Within 12 months of confirmation by members
compliances.note: The page was last modified 2022-07-21.

compliances.name: File financial statements (federal soliciting not-for-profit)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A federal not-for-profit corporation that receives more than $10,000 in public donations or government grants in a single financial year sends its financial statements to Corporations Canada every year. Filing is free.
compliances.why: It is a federal not-for-profit corporation that received more than $10,000 from public donations or government grants in one financial year.
compliances.appliesInWords: Soliciting corporations under the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act.

due.text: Not less than 21 days before each annual meeting of members

compliances.dueText: Not less than 21 days before each annual meeting of members or as soon as possible after a written resolution is signed.
compliances.penalty: Any not-for-profit corporation that defaults for a period of one year in sending any fee, notice or document required by the NFP Act could be dissolved.
compliances.evidence: Not less than 21 days before each annual meeting of members or as soon as possible after a written resolution is signed
compliances.note: The page was last modified 2022-07-21.

compliances.name: Record of Employment
compliances.head: Employment records
compliances.brief: Each time an employee has an interruption of earnings (seven days in a row with no work and no insurable earnings), the employer issues a Record of Employment. It is the record used for the employee's Employment Insurance claim.
compliances.why: You pay employees.
compliances.appliesInWords: Every employer whose employee has an interruption of earnings: seven consecutive calendar days with no work and no insurable earnings, or the start of wage-loss insurance payments.

due.text: Within 5 calendar days of the interruption of earnings (paper), or of the end of the pay period in which it happens (electronic)

compliances.dueText: Paper ROE: within 5 calendar days of the first day of the interruption of earnings, or of the day you become aware of it. Electronic ROE with weekly, biweekly or semi-monthly pay: up to 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the interruption occurs. Electronic ROE with monthly pay or 13 pay periods a year: the earlier of 5 calendar days after the end of that pay period and 15 calendar days after the first day of the interruption.
compliances.penalty: The page states a consequence only for false reasons: if you knowingly enter a false or misleading reason for issuing an ROE, you may be subject to fines or prosecution.
compliances.evidence: If you issue ROEs on paper, you must issue an ROE within 5 calendar days of: the first day of an interruption of earnings ...
compliances.note: Keep records of the serial numbers of all completed or destroyed ROEs for 6 years. The page does not state the penalty for a late ROE.

compliances.name: Pay equity annual statement (federally regulated employers)
compliances.form: Annual statement to the Pay Equity Commissioner
compliances.head: Pay and equity reports
compliances.authority: Pay Equity Commissioner (Canadian Human Rights Commission)
compliances.brief: Federally regulated employers with 10 or more employees must have a pay equity plan and send the Pay Equity Commissioner a statement about it every year, even when the plan has not changed.
compliances.why: You are a federally regulated employer with 10 or more employees.
compliances.appliesInWords: Federally regulated workplaces with an average of 10 or more employees.
compliances.dueText: Employers must submit an annual statement by June 30 each year, even if their pay equity plan hasn't changed. The first statement is due by June 30 of the calendar year after the employer posted its final pay equity plan.
compliances.penalty: The page states no penalty for a late statement. Knowingly making a false or misleading statement is described as a very serious offence that could lead to an administrative monetary penalty.
compliances.evidence: Employers must submit an annual statement by June 30 each year, even if their pay equity plan hasn't changed.
compliances.note: The final pay equity plan itself is due three years after the employer becomes subject to the Act (September 3, 2024 for employers covered on August 31, 2021), and a revised plan is posted by the fifth anniversary of posting. The 10-employee threshold was read on 'Overview of the Pay Equity Act' (canada.ca, 2023-11-28).

compliances.name: Employment equity annual report (federally regulated, 100 or more employees)
compliances.head: Pay and equity reports
compliances.authority: Employment and Social Development Canada (Labour Program)
compliances.brief: Federally regulated private-sector employers and Crown corporations with 100 or more employees send the Labour Program an employment equity report every year.
compliances.why: You are a federally regulated employer with 100 or more employees.
compliances.appliesInWords: Federally regulated private-sector employers and Crown corporations that have 100 or more employees (the Legislated Employment Equity Program).
compliances.dueText: Every year by June 1, employers submit employment equity reports to the Labour Program.
compliances.evidence: Every year by June 1, over 500 of these employers submit employment equity reports to the Labour Program.
compliances.note: The page read is dated 2022-08-25 and does not state the penalty or the period the report covers.

compliances.name: Employer's Annual Hazardous Occurrence Report (federally regulated employers)
compliances.head: Yearly safety reports
compliances.authority: Employment and Social Development Canada (Labour Program)
compliances.brief: Employers under federal jurisdiction report to the Labour Program every year on the injuries and other hazardous occurrences in their workplaces during the previous calendar year.
compliances.why: You are a federally regulated employer with staff.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers subject to federal jurisdiction and regulated by the Canada Labour Code. An owner operator who had no staff in the previous calendar year does not file it.
compliances.dueText: Each year by March 1, for January 1 to December 31 of the previous year.
compliances.evidence: Each year by March 1, employers subject to federal jurisdiction and regulated by the Canada Labour Code
compliances.note: The pages read do not state the penalty or say in so many words that a nil report is required. A third report, the Work Place Committee Report, is also due March 1; which employers must file it was not on the pages read.

compliances.name: Employer's Annual Harassment and Violence Occurrence Report (federally regulated employers)
compliances.head: Yearly safety reports
compliances.authority: Employment and Social Development Canada (Labour Program)
compliances.brief: Employers under federal jurisdiction report to the Labour Program every year on the occurrences of workplace harassment and violence for which they received a notice during the previous calendar year.
compliances.why: You are a federally regulated employer with staff.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers subject to federal jurisdiction and regulated by the Canada Labour Code.
compliances.dueText: All three reports (EAHOR, EAHVOR and the Work Place Committee Report) are due by March 1st of each year, for the previous calendar year.
compliances.evidence: All three reports are due by March 1st of each year.
compliances.note: Who must submit was read on 'Employer's Annual Health and Safety Reports: Who must submit' (2025-12-30). The pages read do not state the penalty.

compliances.name: Accessibility plan and progress reports (federally regulated, 10 or more employees)
compliances.form: Accessibility plan, progress report and feedback process
compliances.head: Accessibility
compliances.brief: Federally regulated businesses with 10 or more employees publish an accessibility plan, report on their progress in the years between plans, and tell the Accessibility Commissioner each time they publish.
compliances.why: You are a federally regulated business with 10 or more employees.
compliances.appliesInWords: Federally regulated private-sector businesses with an average of 10 or more employees. Businesses with 9 or fewer employees are exempt.
compliances.dueText: First accessibility plans were due June 1, 2023 for businesses with 100 or more employees and June 1, 2024 for businesses with 10 to 99 employees. Publish progress reports by the first and second anniversary of that deadline, and update and publish the plan every 3 years. Tell the Accessibility Commissioner within 48 hours after publishing any of these documents.
compliances.penalty: The penalty amount for very serious violations could be as small as $6,250 and as big as $250,000.
compliances.evidence: Small businesses with 10 to 99 employees must prepare and publish their first accessibility plans by June 1, 2024
compliances.note: Deadlines can differ for businesses that fall under the CRTC's or the Canadian Transportation Agency's accessibility rules. The summary page is dated 2023-06-16.

compliances.name: Report a privacy breach and keep breach records (PIPEDA)
compliances.form: Breach report to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
compliances.head: Privacy breaches
compliances.authority: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
compliances.brief: When personal information is lost, stolen or accessed without permission and this creates a real risk of significant harm to someone, the organization reports it to the Privacy Commissioner and tells the people affected. A record of every breach, serious or not, is kept for two years.
compliances.why: Your business holds personal information about people.
compliances.appliesInWords: Organizations subject to the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA).

due.text: As soon as feasible after you determine a breach creates a real risk of significant harm

compliances.dueText: Notification to individuals must be given as soon as feasible after you have determined that a breach of security safeguards involving a real risk of significant harm has occurred, and the breach must be reported to the Privacy Commissioner. Keep records of all breaches of security safeguards for two years.
compliances.penalty: It is an offence to knowingly contravene PIPEDA's reporting, notification and record-keeping requirements, and doing so could lead to fines. The Commissioner can refer possible offences to the Attorney General of Canada.
compliances.evidence: The law requires you to keep breach records of all breaches of security safeguards for two years.
compliances.note: The page gives the 'as soon as feasible' timing for notifying individuals; it does not state a separate number of days for the report to the Commissioner, and it does not state the fine amount. Alberta, British Columbia and Québec have their own private-sector privacy laws for information handled within the province.

compliances.name: Act on unsubscribe requests and identify yourself in commercial emails and texts (CASL)
compliances.head: Anti-spam
compliances.brief: A business that sends commercial emails or texts needs the recipient's consent, must say who it is and how to reach it, and must include a working way to unsubscribe.
compliances.why: You send commercial emails, texts or other electronic messages.
compliances.appliesInWords: Businesses that send commercial electronic messages, such as emails and texts, to customers or prospects.

due.text: Within 10 business days of each unsubscribe request

compliances.dueText: Every unsubscribe request must be actioned within 10 business days or less and at no cost to the recipient. The contact information in each message must be valid for at least 60 days after you send it. Implied consent may be valid for up to 2 years, or just 6 months in the case of inquiries or applications.
compliances.evidence: every unsubscribe request must be actioned within 10 business days or less and at no cost to the recipient
compliances.note: The CRTC's own pages (crtc.gc.ca) refused automated access, so the penalty amounts were not read and are left out. The ISED page read is dated 2019-04-01.

compliances.name: Large Cash Transaction Report
compliances.head: FINTRAC reports
compliances.brief: A business in a FINTRAC-regulated sector reports every time it receives $10,000 or more in cash in a single transaction, or in linked amounts within 24 hours.
compliances.why: Your business is in a sector that must report to FINTRAC.
compliances.appliesInWords: All reporting entities: for example accountants, real estate brokers and developers, dealers in precious metals and stones, money services businesses, mortgage brokers and lenders, securities dealers, life insurers, casinos and financial entities.

due.text: Within 15 calendar days after the day you receive the cash

compliances.dueText: Within 15 calendar days after the day on which you receive the cash. A report is required when you receive $10,000 or more in cash in a single transaction, or 2 or more amounts in cash that total $10,000 or more within a consecutive 24-hour window.
compliances.penalty: Failure to provide applicable reporting information will result in non-compliance and may lead to criminal or administrative penalties.
compliances.evidence: within 15 calendar days after the day on which you receive the cash
compliances.note: Accountants, real estate businesses and British Columbia notaries are covered only when carrying out certain activities for clients; FINTRAC's sector pages set these out.

compliances.name: Suspicious Transaction Report
compliances.head: FINTRAC reports
compliances.brief: A business in a FINTRAC-regulated sector, and its employees, must report suspicious transactions to FINTRAC.
compliances.why: Your business is in a sector that must report to FINTRAC.
compliances.appliesInWords: All reporting entities and their employees.

due.text: As soon as practicable after you have completed the measures that support your suspicion

compliances.dueText: You must submit the Suspicious Transaction Report to FINTRAC as soon as practicable after you have completed measures (the page's sentence continues with what those measures are). There is no fixed number of days.
compliances.evidence: You must submit the Suspicious Transaction Report to FINTRAC as soon as practicable after you have completed measures
compliances.note: The page is very long and only its first part was read. What makes a transaction suspicious, and the measures the deadline is counted from, are set out there.

compliances.name: Review your anti-money-laundering compliance program
compliances.head: FINTRAC compliance program
compliances.brief: Every business in a FINTRAC-regulated sector must have a compliance program with a named compliance officer, and must test how well the program works at least every two years.
compliances.why: Your business is in a sector that must report to FINTRAC.
compliances.appliesInWords: All reporting entities.

due.text: At least every two years; report the results to a senior officer within 30 days

compliances.dueText: Carry out this review every two years at a minimum. If you are an entity, report the results in writing to a senior officer no later than 30 days after the completion of the effectiveness review.
compliances.penalty: FINTRAC may issue administrative monetary penalties (civil penalties) to reporting entities for non-compliance. The amounts are on a separate page that was not read.
compliances.evidence: All reporting entities must establish and implement a compliance program. ... carry out this review every two years at a minimum.

compliances.name: Money services business registration: renew and keep up to date
compliances.head: FINTRAC registration
compliances.brief: A money services business registers with FINTRAC before it begins to operate, renews the registration every two years and reports changes to its details.
compliances.why: It is a money services business.
compliances.appliesInWords: Money services businesses operating in Canada, and foreign money services businesses that direct and provide services to clients in Canada.

due.text: Renew before the registration expires (every two years); report changes within 30 days

compliances.dueText: Your registration is valid for two years. You must renew your registration before its expiry date. If registration information changes you must inform FINTRAC within 30 days, and you have 30 days to respond to a clarification request.
compliances.penalty: Failure to register may result in administrative monetary penalties or criminal charges. Failure to respond to a clarification request on time may result in the same, and FINTRAC can deny or revoke the registration.
compliances.evidence: Your registration is valid for two years. You must renew your registration before its expiry date.

compliances.name: Electronic Funds Transfer Report (money services businesses)
compliances.head: FINTRAC reports
compliances.brief: A money services business reports each international electronic funds transfer of $10,000 or more.
compliances.why: It is a money services business.
compliances.appliesInWords: Financial entities, money services businesses and foreign money services businesses, and casinos.

due.text: Within 5 business days of the transfer

compliances.dueText: You must submit an Electronic Funds Transfer Report to FINTRAC within 5 business days. It covers an international electronic funds transfer of $10,000 or more in a single transaction.
compliances.evidence: You must submit an Electronic Funds Transfer Report to FINTRAC within 5 business days
compliances.note: Only the first part of this long page was read: the day from which the 5 business days are counted, and the 24-hour rule for linked transfers, should be confirmed there. Banks, credit unions and casinos owe the same report but are outside this checker's entity types.

compliances.name: Import-export program account (RM) with the border agency
compliances.form: RM account, registered in the CARM Client Portal
compliances.head: Import and export registration
compliances.brief: A business that imports or exports commercial goods needs an import-export program (RM) account on its business number. New importers and exporters register for it in the CARM Client Portal of the Canada Border Services Agency.
compliances.why: You import or export commercial goods.
compliances.appliesInWords: Any business that imports commercial goods into Canada or exports them from Canada.

due.text: Before your first import or export, well in advance

compliances.dueText: Ensure you have registered for an RM account well in advance of your import or export deadlines.
compliances.penalty: No penalty is stated. The page says registering early helps avoid delays in the release of your goods.
compliances.evidence: If your business imports or exports commercial goods into or out of Canada ... you need to have an import-export program (RM) account.
compliances.note: Not read on an official page and therefore left out: the due dates for paying duties and taxes on statements of account, the deadline for the commercial accounting declaration, and the financial security rules for release prior to payment.

compliances.name: Investment Canada Act notification (foreign investors)
compliances.form: Notification – establishment of a new business or acquisition of control
compliances.head: Foreign investment
compliances.authority: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (Investment Review)
compliances.brief: A non-Canadian files a notification each time it starts a new business activity in Canada or acquires control of an existing Canadian business, unless the investment is one that needs a full review.
compliances.why: The business is owned or controlled by non-Canadians and has started a new business activity in Canada or bought control of a Canadian business.
compliances.appliesInWords: Non-Canadians establishing a new Canadian business or acquiring control of an existing one, where the transaction is not reviewable.

due.text: No later than 30 days after the investment is implemented

compliances.dueText: A Notification must be filed no later than thirty days after the implementation of the investment.
compliances.evidence: A Notification must be filed no later than thirty days after the implementation of the investment.
compliances.note: The page read is dated 2023-09-28. It does not state a penalty for failing to notify.

compliances.name: Renew a registered trademark
compliances.head: Renewals
compliances.brief: A trademark registration is renewed for 10 years at a time by paying a renewal fee, which depends on the number of classes of goods or services.
compliances.why: You or your business own a trademark registered in Canada.
compliances.appliesInWords: Owners of trademarks registered in Canada.

due.text: From 6 months before to 6 months after the registration expires

compliances.dueText: A renewal fee must be submitted no earlier than 6 months before the expiry of the initial period or renewal period and no later than 6 months after it or, if later, two months after a renewal notice.
compliances.evidence: a renewal fee must be submitted no earlier than 6 months before the expiry of the initial period or renewal period
compliances.note: The practice notice read is dated 2020-10-27. It does not set out in general terms what happens when a registration is not renewed, so no consequence is given here.

compliances.name: Forced labour and child labour in supply chains: annual report
compliances.form: Report to the Minister of Public Safety (online questionnaire and report)
compliances.head: Supply chain
compliances.brief: Large businesses that make goods, import goods made outside Canada, or control a business that does, submit a report every year under the Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act and publish it on their website.
compliances.why: It is a large business that produces or imports goods, or controls one that does.
compliances.appliesInWords: A corporation, trust, partnership or other unincorporated organization that is listed on a stock exchange in Canada, or that has a place of business, does business or has assets in Canada and meets at least two of three size tests for at least one of its two most recent financial years ($20 million or more in assets, $40 million or more in revenue, an average of 250 or more employees), and that produces goods in Canada or elsewhere, imports goods produced outside Canada, or controls an entity that does.
compliances.dueText: A report must be submitted to the Minister of Public Safety by May 31 of each year, covering the entity's previous financial year, and published in a prominent location on the entity's website.
compliances.evidence: Certain entities and government institutions must submit a report to the Minister of Public Safety by May 31 of each year.
compliances.note: The pages read do not state the fine for failing to report. The report must be approved by the entity's governing body and carry an attestation.

compliances.name: Answer mandatory Statistics Canada business surveys
compliances.head: Statistical surveys
compliances.brief: When Statistics Canada selects a business for one of its business surveys, taking part is in most cases a legal duty, not a choice.
compliances.why: You run a business that Statistics Canada may select for a survey.
compliances.appliesInWords: Any business or farm that Statistics Canada contacts for a mandatory survey.

due.text: By the date given on the survey you receive

compliances.dueText: Participation in most business and agricultural surveys is mandatory. The date to reply by is given with each survey.
compliances.evidence: Additionally, participation in most business and agricultural surveys is mandatory.
compliances.note: NOT CONFIRMED: the page read states that participation is mandatory but gives no reply deadline and no penalty. Statistics Canada's business survey pages (statcan.gc.ca/en/survey/business and /mandatory) returned HTTP 503 on 2026-11-11, so the wording that the reply date is on each survey is an assumption, not a quotation.

compliances.name: Pension plan annual information return (federally registered plans)
compliances.form: OSFI 49, OSFI 49A and the Pension Plan Annual Corporate Certification
compliances.head: Pension plans
compliances.authority: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
compliances.brief: The administrator of a pension plan registered under the federal Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 files a yearly information return and certification with OSFI, through its Regulatory Reporting System.
compliances.why: The business administers a pension plan registered with OSFI.
compliances.appliesInWords: The administrator (or its agent) of a federally regulated private pension plan registered, or filed for registration, under the Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985, while assets remain in the pension fund.

due.text: Within six months after the end of the plan year

compliances.dueText: The returns must be filed within six months after the end of the plan year to which they relate.
compliances.penalty: Plans may be subject to CRA late filing penalties if the filing process is incomplete, because the information reaches the Canada Revenue Agency only after the returns are accepted.
compliances.evidence: must be filed within six months after the end of the plan year to which they relate
compliances.note: The plan year may differ from the business's financial year, so no date is worked out. Plans registered with a province (for example with Ontario's FSRA, whose site refused automated access) have their own return and deadline, not covered here.

compliances.name: National Pollutant Release Inventory report
compliances.head: Environment
compliances.brief: Facilities that meet the size and substance tests report to the National Pollutant Release Inventory every year. Reporting is mandatory under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999.
compliances.why: One of your facilities meets the inventory's reporting criteria.
compliances.appliesInWords: Owners or operators of facilities where employees and contractors work more than 20,000 hours during a year (about 10 full-time workers) and a listed substance is made, processed, used or released above its threshold. Some activities, such as operating stationary combustion equipment above the air-release thresholds, are reportable regardless of employee hours.
compliances.dueText: Reports are due every year by June 1, for the previous calendar year (2026 calendar year: the deadline is June 1, 2027).
compliances.evidence: Reports are due every year by June 1.
compliances.note: The pages read do not state the penalty. The year-by-year deadlines were read on 'Deadlines and changes: reporting guide for the National Pollutant Release Inventory' (2025-07-22).

compliances.name: Ontario accessibility compliance report
compliances.head: Accessibility
compliances.brief: Ontario businesses and non-profit organizations with 20 or more employees file an accessibility compliance report every three years.
compliances.why: You have 20 or more employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: A business or non-profit organization with 20 or more employees in Ontario. Designated public-sector organizations report every two years.
compliances.dueText: You must file an accessibility compliance report every three years. The reporting deadline is December 31, 2026.
compliances.penalty: If you do not file, you could face enforcement measures which can include financial penalties.
compliances.evidence: The reporting deadline is December 31, 2026.
compliances.note: The three-year cycle cannot be written as a yearly rule: only the 2026 date read on the page is given. After it, the next report follows three years later; confirm the date on the page. The page does not say how employees are counted.

compliances.name: Give each new employee Ontario's employment standards poster
compliances.head: Mandatory posters
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: Ontario employers give every employee a copy of the official employment standards poster. Workplaces also post the Health & Safety at Work poster, a copy of the Occupational Health and Safety Act and the WSIB 'In case of injury' poster (Form 82).
compliances.why: You pay employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers of employees covered by Ontario's Employment Standards Act.

due.text: Within 30 days of each employee's date of hire

compliances.dueText: The poster must be provided to employees who are covered by the ESA within 30 days of their date of hire.
compliances.evidence: must be provided to employees who are covered by the ESA within 30 days of their date of hire.
compliances.note: Federally regulated employers follow the Canada Labour Code instead.

compliances.name: Ontario written policy on disconnecting from work
compliances.head: Written workplace policies
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: Ontario employers with 25 or more employees on January 1 must have a written policy on disconnecting from work and give every employee a copy.
compliances.why: You have 25 or more employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers that employ 25 or more employees in Ontario on January 1 of the year. Part-time and casual employees each count as one.
compliances.dueText: The policy must be in place before March 1 of that year. A copy must be provided to employees within 30 calendar days of the policy being prepared or changed. Keep each policy for three years after it is no longer in effect.
compliances.evidence: Employers that employ 25 or more employees are required to have a written policy on disconnecting from work ... in place before March 1 of that year
compliances.note: The date shown is February 28: the policy has to exist before March 1, so the last day of February is the last day to have it in place (February 29 in a leap year).

compliances.name: Ontario written policy on electronic monitoring of employees
compliances.head: Written workplace policies
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: Ontario employers with 25 or more employees on January 1 must have a written policy saying whether and how they electronically monitor employees, and give every employee a copy.
compliances.why: You have 25 or more employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers that employ 25 or more employees in Ontario on January 1 of any year.
compliances.dueText: The policy must be in place before March 1 of that year. A copy must be provided to employees within 30 calendar days. Keep every policy for three years after it is no longer in effect.
compliances.evidence: must have a written policy on the electronic monitoring of employees in place before March 1 of that year
compliances.note: The date shown is February 28: the policy has to exist before March 1, so the last day of February is the last day to have it in place (February 29 in a leap year).

compliances.name: Report a workplace injury or illness to the WSIB (Ontario)
compliances.head: Injury reporting
compliances.brief: An Ontario employer reports a work injury or illness to the WSIB when the employee needs treatment from a health professional beyond first aid, cannot go to work, is paid less or works fewer hours, or needs modified work at regular pay for more than seven calendar days. The employee gets a copy.
compliances.why: You pay employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Ontario employers covered by the WSIB.

due.text: Within three business days of learning about the injury or illness

compliances.dueText: You must report a workplace injury or illness within three business days of learning about it. The WSIB must receive the Employer's report of injury (Form 7) within three business days.
compliances.penalty: You could face a financial penalty as well as prosecution for not reporting or reporting late.
compliances.evidence: You must report a workplace injury or illness within three business days of learning about it if your employee:
compliances.note: No report is needed when first aid was enough, no time was lost and pay did not change (and any modified work lasted seven days or less).

compliances.name: Notify Ontario's ministry of a workplace death, critical injury or occupational illness
compliances.form: Notice and written report under the Occupational Health and Safety Act
compliances.head: Serious incidents
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: When someone is killed or critically injured at an Ontario workplace, the employer tells the ministry, the joint health and safety committee or representative and the union at once, then follows up in writing. Other accidents and occupational illnesses have a four-day written notice.
compliances.why: You pay employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers and constructors under Ontario's Occupational Health and Safety Act.

due.text: Immediately, then a written report within 48 hours

compliances.dueText: Fatality or critical injury: immediately notify the ministry's Health and Safety Contact Centre, the joint health and safety committee or representative and the union, and provide a written report within 48 hours. Other accidents, explosions, fires or workplace violence: written notice within four days of the incident to the committee or representative and the union (to the ministry only if an inspector requires it). Occupational illness: written notice to the ministry within four days of being advised.
compliances.evidence: must provide a written report within 48 hours
compliances.note: The page does not state the penalty.

compliances.name: Ontario joint health and safety committee: meetings and inspections
compliances.head: Safety committees
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: An Ontario workplace that regularly employs 20 or more workers must have a joint health and safety committee. It meets and inspects the workplace on a fixed cycle, and its certified members refresh their training every three years.
compliances.why: You regularly employ 20 or more workers in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Any Ontario workplace that regularly employs 20 or more workers. A workplace with 6 to 19 workers needs one health and safety representative chosen by the workers instead.

due.text: Meet at least once every three months; inspect the workplace at least once a month

compliances.dueText: Committee members are required to meet at least once every three months. The workplace must be inspected at least once a month. Certified members complete refresher training every 3 years.
compliances.evidence: Committee members are required to meet at least once every three months.
compliances.note: The page does not state the penalty. Names and work locations of committee members must be posted in the workplace.

compliances.name: Review Ontario health and safety, workplace violence and harassment policies every year
compliances.form: Written policies under the Occupational Health and Safety Act
compliances.head: Written workplace policies
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: Ontario workplaces with more than 5 regularly employed workers must post their health and safety policy and their workplace violence and workplace harassment policies, and review them at least once a year.
compliances.why: You regularly employ more than 5 workers in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Ontario workplaces with more than 5 regularly employed workers.

due.text: At least once a year

compliances.dueText: These policies must be reviewed at least once a year.
compliances.evidence: at least once a year
compliances.note: Read on Ontario's page 'Posters required in the workplace'. Smaller workplaces still need the policies; the page ties the posting duty to more than 5 workers.

compliances.name: Ontario health and safety awareness training for new supervisors and workers
compliances.form: Basic occupational health and safety awareness training
compliances.head: Mandatory training
compliances.authority: Government of Ontario (ministry responsible for labour)
compliances.brief: Ontario employers make sure every worker and every supervisor completes a basic health and safety awareness program, and keep a record of it. Owners who supervise workers count as supervisors.
compliances.why: You pay employees in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Ontario employers, for all workers and for anyone who meets the Occupational Health and Safety Act definition of supervisor, including people who supervise only temporarily.

due.text: Supervisors: within one week of starting to supervise. Workers: as soon as practicable

compliances.dueText: Employers must ensure supervisors complete an awareness training program for supervisors within one week of performing work as a supervisor. Employers must ensure workers complete an awareness training program for workers as soon as practicable.
compliances.evidence: Employers must ensure supervisors complete an awareness training program for supervisors within one week
compliances.note: The worker rule was read on the companion page 'Worker awareness training program' (updated 2024-04-11).

compliances.name: Ontario initial return for a new corporation
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A new Ontario corporation files an initial return listing its directors, its five most senior officers and its registered office address. There is no government fee when filed online with ServiceOntario.
compliances.why: It is a corporation in Ontario that was not incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Ontario business and not-for-profit corporations. Corporations from outside Ontario that carry on business there file their own version, under a separate notice.

due.text: Within 60 days after incorporation, amalgamation or continuation

compliances.dueText: Within 60 days after the date of incorporation, amalgamation or continuation of the corporation.
compliances.penalty: Sections 13 and 14 of the Corporations Information Act provide penalties. A corporation in default that has unpaid fines or penalties cannot maintain a proceeding in an Ontario court in respect of its business.
compliances.evidence: Ontario corporations must file an Initial Return under the Corporations Information Act (CIA) setting out the prescribed information within 60 days after the date of incorporation, amalgamation or continuation of the corporation
compliances.note: Federal and other out-of-province corporations operating in Ontario file their own initial return, shown as a separate item (within 60 days after beginning to carry on business in Ontario).

compliances.name: Ontario initial return for a federal corporation
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A corporation incorporated outside Ontario, a federal corporation included, that carries on business in Ontario files an Initial Return under Ontario's Corporations Information Act with the Ontario Business Registry. It has no fee. Changes are then reported by a Notice of Change.
compliances.why: It is a federal corporation in Ontario.
compliances.appliesInWords: Extra-provincial corporations carrying on business in Ontario: the notice says the Act's filing requirements 'apply to all corporations with or without share capital wherever or however incorporated and includes an extra-provincial corporation'.

due.text: Within 60 days after the corporation begins to carry on business in Ontario

compliances.dueText: Within 60 days after the date the corporation begins to carry on business in Ontario.
compliances.penalty: Sections 13 and 14 of the Corporations Information Act provide penalties. A corporation in default that has unpaid fines or penalties cannot maintain a proceeding in an Ontario court in respect of its business.
compliances.evidence: Extra-provincial corporations must file an Initial Return under the Corporations Information Act (CIA) setting out the prescribed information within 60 days after the date the corporation begins to carry on business in Ontario (section 3 of the CIA). After an Initial Return has been filed, the corporations must file a Notice of Change for any change in the information previously filed within 15 days after the change takes place (section 4 of the CIA).
compliances.note: Read in Ontario's notice for extra-provincial corporations, effective October 19, 2021. Ontario's yearly return is not asked of federal corporations: its notice lists Ontario corporations and licensed foreign corporations only.

compliances.name: Ontario notice of change (directors, officers, address)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: An Ontario corporation reports every change to the information it has filed, such as its registered office address, its directors or its five most senior officers.
compliances.why: It is a corporation in Ontario, wherever it was incorporated.
compliances.appliesInWords: Ontario business and not-for-profit corporations that have filed an initial return.

due.text: Within 15 days after the change takes place

compliances.dueText: Corporations must file a Notice of Change for every change in the information filed, within 15 days after the day the change takes place.
compliances.penalty: Sections 13 and 14 of the Corporations Information Act provide penalties. A corporation in default that has unpaid fines or penalties cannot maintain a proceeding in an Ontario court in respect of its business.
compliances.evidence: corporations must file a Notice of Change for every change in the information filed under the CIA, within 15 days after the day the change takes place
compliances.note: Ontario's Business Registry page (updated 2026-09-28) says the same of every registered entity: 'If your entity's information has changed, you must tell the ministry within 15 days.' Limited partnerships file a declaration of change and business-name holders an amended registration. Federal and other out-of-province corporations are covered too: the notice for extra-provincial corporations (effective October 19, 2021) says 'CIA filing requirements apply to all corporations with or without share capital wherever or however incorporated and includes an extra-provincial corporation' and gives the same 15 days.

compliances.name: Ontario register of individuals with significant control
compliances.form: Register kept at the registered office (not filed)
compliances.head: Ownership register
compliances.brief: Privately held Ontario corporations keep a record of the individuals who own or control them at the registered office. It is not sent to a registry, but must be shown to law enforcement, tax and certain regulatory authorities on request.
compliances.why: It is a private corporation in Ontario that was not incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Privately-held corporations in Ontario. Public corporations and their wholly-owned subsidiaries are exempt.

due.text: Update at least once a year, and within 15 days of learning of a change

compliances.dueText: Records must be updated at least once a year, and within 15 days of the corporation becoming aware of a change. The requirement took effect January 1, 2023.
compliances.evidence: privately-held corporations in Ontario are required to keep their beneficial ownership information
compliances.note: The page is dated 2022-12-23 and does not state the fines.

compliances.name: Québec current updating declaration (changes during the year)
compliances.form: Déclaration de mise à jour courante (enterprise register)
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A business registered in Québec's enterprise register reports any change to its file during the year, for example a new address or a change of directors. Filing is free.
compliances.why: The business is registered in Québec's enterprise register.
compliances.appliesInWords: Every enterprise registered in Québec's enterprise register, once its annual updating declaration has been filed for the year.

due.text: Within 30 days following any change

compliances.dueText: Enterprises have 30 days following any change to file a current updating declaration.
compliances.evidence: 30 days following any change to file a current updating declaration
compliances.note: Sanctions are on a separate page ('Civil and Penal Sanctions Stemming from Registration') that was not read. Information on ultimate beneficiaries (the people who own or control the business) is declared in the same declarations since March 31, 2023; that the 30-day rule covers a change of ultimate beneficiary was seen only in a search summary.

compliances.name: Register with the Office québécois de la langue française (25 or more employees)
compliances.head: French language
compliances.authority: Office québécois de la langue française
compliances.brief: A business that employs 25 or more people in Québec for six months registers with the Office québécois de la langue française and then reports on how French is used in the business. If French is not in general use, the Office asks for a francization program.
compliances.why: You employ 25 or more people in Québec.
compliances.appliesInWords: Businesses that employ 25 or more people in Québec during a period of 6 months.

due.text: Within 6 months after the end of the 6-month period with 25 or more employees

compliances.dueText: Register with the Office within the 6 months following the end of that period. Within three months of the date the registration certificate is issued, send the Office an analysis of the use of French in the business. If a francization program is requested, submit it within three months, then report on it every 12 months.
compliances.evidence: doivent s'inscrire à l'Office québécois de la langue française dans les 6 mois suivant la fin de cette période
compliances.note: The steps after registration were read on the OQLF page 'Entreprises' (updated 2026-10-23). Neither page states the fines. Businesses with 25 or more employees must show proof of compliance to obtain public contracts or subsidies. In a business with 100 or more employees the francization committee prepares the program.

compliances.name: Report a confidentiality incident and keep an incident register (Québec)
compliances.form: Avis à la Commission d'accès à l'information
compliances.head: Privacy breaches
compliances.authority: Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec
compliances.brief: When personal information held by a Québec business is accessed, used, disclosed or lost without authorization and there is a risk of serious harm, the business promptly notifies the Commission in writing. Every incident, serious or not, is entered in a register.
compliances.why: Your business holds personal information about people and operates in Québec.
compliances.appliesInWords: Every enterprise carrying on business in Québec that holds personal information.

due.text: Promptly after an incident that presents a risk of serious harm

compliances.dueText: When an incident presents a risk of serious harm, the enterprise must promptly notify the Commission in writing (« l'entreprise doit s'empresser d'en aviser la Commission »). The information in the register must be kept up to date and kept for a minimum of five years.
compliances.penalty: The page describes no fine. The Commission may order the enterprise to notify the people concerned.
compliances.evidence: Les renseignements du registre doivent être mis à jour et conservés pour une période minimale de cinq ans
compliances.note: The people concerned must also be told. No number of days is given: the law's word is prompt. The first sentence of 'brief' describes an incident in general terms and is not a quotation.

compliances.name: Québec pay equity declaration (DEMES)
compliances.form: Déclaration de l'employeur en matière d'équité salariale
compliances.head: Pay and equity reports
compliances.brief: Québec employers covered by the Pay Equity Act declare each year to the CNESST where they stand with their pay equity work.
compliances.why: You have 10 or more employees in Québec.
compliances.appliesInWords: Reported, not confirmed: employers registered in Québec's enterprise register that declared 11 or more employees there the year before, and employers that have already declared they are subject to the Pay Equity Act (which applies from an average of 10 employees).

due.text: Every year: the period could not be confirmed (reported as within 6 months after the end of the financial year)

compliances.dueText: Reported, not confirmed: private employers file the declaration within 6 months after the end of their financial year, in the same period as the annual updating declaration to the enterprise register.
compliances.evidence: Not read: the CNESST site returned HTTP 403 to every request on 2026-11-11.
compliances.note: NOT CONFIRMED, so no date is worked out. The CNESST site refused automated access (HTTP 403) again on 2026-11-12, so the threshold, the deadline and the fines were seen only in a search engine's summary of CNESST pages. Confirm on cnesst.gouv.qc.ca before use.

compliances.name: British Columbia transparency register: yearly review and updates
compliances.form: Transparency register (kept at the records office, not filed)
compliances.head: Ownership register
compliances.brief: A private company incorporated in British Columbia keeps a register of its significant individuals (the people who own or control it) at its records office, confirms it once a year and updates it when it learns something new.
compliances.why: It is a private company incorporated in British Columbia.
compliances.appliesInWords: Private companies incorporated in B.C.: companies that are not reporting issuers, not listed on a designated stock exchange and not in an exempt class.
compliances.dueText: Every year, within the period starting on the anniversary of the date on which the company was recognized and ending 2 months after that date, take reasonable steps to confirm the register is accurate, complete and up to date. New information must be recorded within 30 days after the company becomes aware of it.
compliances.evidence: must record that information in its transparency register within 30 days after becoming aware of the information
compliances.note: Read in the Business Corporations Act (BC Laws, current to November 3, 2026) and on the province's 'Transparency Register' page (last updated 2022-09-01). The part read has no requirement to file the register with the government and no fine amounts; a 2023 bill proposed both a filing duty and a shorter update period, and whether it is in force was not confirmed.

compliances.name: British Columbia notice of change of directors
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: A B.C. company files a notice with the registrar when its directors change or a director's address changes. A separate notice is needed for each date of change. The filing fee is $20 plus a $1.50 service fee.
compliances.why: It is a company incorporated in British Columbia.
compliances.appliesInWords: Companies under British Columbia's Business Corporations Act.

due.text: Within 15 days after the change

compliances.dueText: A company must, within 15 days after the date of change in its directors or in the address of any of its directors, file a Notice of Change of Directors with the registrar.
compliances.penalty: Failure to comply with the filing requirements of the Business Corporations Act may result in a company being dissolved and struck from the register.
compliances.evidence: A company must, within 15 days after the date of change in its directors or in the address of any of its directors, file a Notice of Change of Directors with the registrar.
compliances.note: The guide is an older document (file last modified 2023-07-27); confirm the fee.

compliances.name: British Columbia pay transparency report
compliances.form: Pay transparency report (Pay Transparency Reporting Tool)
compliances.head: Pay and equity reports
compliances.authority: Government of British Columbia (Ministry of Finance, Gender Equity Office)
compliances.brief: B.C. employers above a set size complete a pay transparency report every year and publish it on a public website.
compliances.why: You have 50 or more employees in British Columbia.
compliances.appliesInWords: Provincially regulated employers with 50 or more employees working in B.C. as of January 1 of the reporting year (1,000 or more from 2024, 300 or more from 2025, 50 or more from 2026). The government's page speaks of 'a provincially regulated employer above a certain size' and says 'Requirements may differ for federally regulated employers', so federally regulated employers are not shown this.
compliances.dueText: Complete the report by November 1 of each year and publish it on a publicly accessible website as soon as practicable. By November 1, 2026: all employers with 50 employees in B.C. or more.
compliances.evidence: By November 1, 2026: all employers with 50 employees in B.C. or more
compliances.note: An employer with no website posts the report in a visible place in each workplace and gives it to anyone who asks. Requirements may differ for federally regulated employers. The page states no penalty.

compliances.name: Report a worker's injury to WorkSafeBC
compliances.form: Employer's Report of Injury or Occupational Disease (Form 7)
compliances.head: Injury reporting
compliances.brief: A B.C. employer reports every injury to a worker that is, or is claimed to be, work-related. A worker's death, a serious injury and certain major incidents must be reported to WorkSafeBC immediately, which the Form 7 does not replace.
compliances.why: You pay employees in British Columbia.
compliances.appliesInWords: Employers covered by British Columbia's Workers Compensation Act.

due.text: Within 3 days after the injury; a death immediately

compliances.dueText: An employer must report to the Board, within 3 days after its occurrence, every injury to a worker. An employer must report immediately to the Board the death of a worker.
compliances.penalty: Employers who do not immediately notify WorkSafeBC of serious incidents may be subject to enforcement, such as an administrative penalty.
compliances.evidence: an employer must report to the Board, within 3 days after its occurrence, every injury to a worker
compliances.note: If the Board has not received the employer's report within a week, it may decide the claim on an interim basis and begin paying compensation.

compliances.name: British Columbia joint health and safety committee: yearly evaluation
compliances.head: Safety committees
compliances.brief: A B.C. workplace with 20 or more workers needs a joint health and safety committee, whose members receive eight hours of training and whose effectiveness is evaluated in writing every year.
compliances.why: You have 20 or more workers in British Columbia.
compliances.appliesInWords: B.C. workplaces with 20 or more workers. A workplace with more than 9 but fewer than 20 workers needs a worker health and safety representative instead.

due.text: A written evaluation once a year

compliances.dueText: A written evaluation must be conducted annually to determine the effectiveness of the joint committee. All joint committee members selected on or after April 3, 2017 must receive eight hours of training and instruction.
compliances.evidence: Section 3.26 of the Regulation requires a written evaluation to be conducted annually to determine the effectiveness of the joint committee.
compliances.note: How often the committee must meet and the deadline for the training were not on the page read.

compliances.name: Report a worker's injury to WCB Alberta
compliances.head: Injury reporting
compliances.brief: An Alberta employer reports an injury or illness that causes lost time or modified work beyond the day of the accident, death or permanent disability, an occupational disease, treatment beyond first aid or medical aid expenses.
compliances.why: You pay employees in Alberta.
compliances.appliesInWords: Alberta employers covered by the Workers' Compensation Act.

due.text: Within 72 hours of being notified of the injury or illness

compliances.dueText: Report to WCB within 72 hours of being notified of an injury or illness. If your worker lost time from work, notify WCB within 24 hours of the worker's return to work. Immediately report fatalities and serious injuries to the OHS Contact Centre, then report the incident to WCB.
compliances.evidence: Report to WCB within 72 hours of being notified of an injury/illness that results in or will likely result in:
compliances.note: Keep a record of every injury or illness, even without first aid, for a minimum of three years. The fact sheet (dated January 17, 2023) does not state the penalty.

compliances.name: Alberta notice of change of directors or address
compliances.form: Change of Director / Change of Address notice
compliances.head: Corporate filings
compliances.brief: An Alberta corporation gives an authorized Corporate Registry service provider its address and director changes, and any change of agent for service. Service providers charge a fee.
compliances.why: It is a corporation in Alberta that was not incorporated federally.
compliances.appliesInWords: Alberta corporations. Out-of-province corporations registered in Alberta have 30 days for head office address or director updates.

due.text: Within 15 days of the change

compliances.dueText: Address or director updates within 15 days of a change, and agent for service updates as soon as they occur.
compliances.penalty: If no new agent for service is appointed within one year of the previous agent's revocation or resignation, the corporation can be dissolved by the Registrar of Corporations.
compliances.evidence: address or director updates within 15 days of a change
compliances.note: Alberta cooperatives have the same 15 days and pay no fee. The page shows no last-updated date.

compliances.name: Notify Alberta's privacy commissioner of a breach (PIPA)
compliances.head: Privacy breaches
compliances.authority: Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Alberta
compliances.brief: An organization in Alberta notifies the Commissioner of a privacy breach when a reasonable person would consider that there is a real risk of significant harm to someone.
compliances.why: Your business holds personal information about people and operates in Alberta.
compliances.appliesInWords: An organization with personal information under its control, under Alberta's Personal Information Protection Act.

due.text: Without unreasonable delay

compliances.dueText: Notify the Commissioner without unreasonable delay where a reasonable person would consider that there exists a real risk of significant harm to an individual.
compliances.evidence: It is mandatory for an organization with personal information under its control to notify the Commissioner
compliances.note: No number of days is set. The page (dated June 2025) does not state the fine.

compliances.name: Alberta unclaimed property: report and hand over
compliances.head: Unclaimed property
compliances.brief: A business that holds property for an owner (a holder) and finds it has gone unclaimed notifies the owner, then reports the property and pays or delivers it to the province.
compliances.why: The business holds unclaimed money or property that belongs to someone else, in Alberta.
compliances.appliesInWords: Holders: a person or entity that is or becomes obligated to hold property, tangible or intangible, for an owner. This includes businesses.
compliances.dueText: Report and remit within 120 days from December 31 of the respective reporting year. Notify property owners between 3 and 8 months prior to transferring the property.
compliances.penalty: A late holder pays interest on the value of the property from the date the holder was required to pay or deliver it.
compliances.evidence: within 120 days from December 31 of the respective reporting year
compliances.note: How long property must sit before it counts as unclaimed depends on its type and was not read. The page shows no last-updated date.
